title: Exploring the Influence of Neuroarchitecture on Human Behavior and Well-being
authors: Joyal George and Vishnu P Prakash, 2024
review_question: To systematically review recent neuroarchitecture research and explore historical evidence on how architecture influences human emotions, behavior, and well-being.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly detailed, but focused on recent neuroarchitecture research and historical evidence on how architecture has been used to influence emotions throughout history.

synthesis_conclusions: Neuroarchitecture explores the powerful connection between design choices in buildings and human well-being, influencing physical health, mental state, emotions, and social interactions.
Architectural elements like light, color, acoustics, material, scale, layout, and volume affect user behavior, emotions, and well-being.
Historical evidence demonstrates that architecture has been used to influence emotions for centuries, even without contemporary neuroscience.
Neuroarchitecture aims to optimize user experience by designing spaces that support cognitive function, emotional well-being, and overall quality of life.
A summary table of neuro-architectural design elements and their impact on human well-being was created, highlighting positive effects.
Design guidelines based on these effects are suggested.
Understanding users' diverse needs, preferences, and behaviors is essential for tailoring effective design solutions.
Neuroarchitecture, by integrating science, technology, health, and arts, can lead to environments that support overall well-being and sustainability.
evidence_gaps: Lack of a comprehensive study on the emotional and cognitive aspects of architecture.
Challenges in designing for diverse groups and addressing specific needs like dementia care.
Need for collaboration between scientists and architects to develop comprehensive tools for architectural design.
More extensive experimental designs and larger sample sizes are recommended to improve results due to inconsistencies in data analysis methods.
Limitations in existing methods focusing on specific environmental stimuli and evaluation systems.
Challenges in explaining experiences solely through physiological terms and accounting for various influencing factors.
Methodological issues stemming from the diversity of stimuli and presentation methods, leading to conflicts in procedures and technical restrictions.
heterogeneity_sources: Inconsistency in data analysis methods used in the studies reviewed.
Inconsistent information gathered from different studies.
Subjectivity of emotional experience, differing person to person.
Individual differences in personality, culture, past experiences, and genetics.
publication_bias: Concern about valuable sources not widely published in traditional sources (gray literature).

moderators.effect: Responses to specific design elements can vary greatly due to differences in personality, culture, past experiences, and genetics.

limitations: Inconsistency in data analysis methods used in the studies reviewed.
The emotional experience is subjective and differs person to person.
Individual responses to design elements vary due to personality, culture, past experiences, and genetics.
The wide scope of the study makes thorough coverage challenging.
Potential for missing valuable sources like gray literature.
Old methods are limited by their focus on specific environmental stimuli and evaluation systems.
Art and architecture are not interchangeable, requiring caution when applying findings from other fields.

Limitations at ontological (breadth of perceptual experiences, unimodal stimuli, subjective beauty/pleasure), epistemological (explaining experiences solely through physiological terms), and methodological (diversity of stimuli, presentation methods, technical restrictions) levels.
Architecture cannot be equated with artistic-aesthetic experiences as it serves broader human needs.
Architecture entails a continuous experience, influenced by transitions and narrative.
Peripheral vision and multisensory engagement are crucial, hindering fragmentation of cognitive-emotional dimension.
Difficulty in achieving universal solutions due to individual differences and environmental factors.

paper_metadata.title: Ecological brain: reframing the study of human behaviour and cognition
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Ecological brain: reframing the study of human behaviour and cognition
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The last decade has seen substantial advances in the capacity to record behaviour and neural activity in humans in real-world settings, to simulate real-world situations in laboratory settings and to apply sophisticated analyses to large-scale data. Along with these developments, a growing number of groups has begun to advocate for real-world neuroscience and cognitive science. Here, we review the arguments and the available methods for real-world research and outline an overarching framework that embeds key ideas proposed in the literature integrating them into a cyclic process of ‘bringing the lab to the real world’ (recording behavioural and neural activity in real-world settings) and ‘bringing the real-world to the lab’ (manipulating the environments in which behaviours occur in the laboratory) that combines exploratory and confirmatory research and is interdisciplinary (including those sciences concerned with the natural, built or virtual environment). We highlight the benefits brought by this framework emphasizing the greater potential for novel discovery, theory development and human-centred applications to the environment.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, thereby improving well-being.
Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which positively impacts health and well-being.
Interacting with natural environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress, leading to improved emotional states.
